column9: Which scientist looked at thin slices of cork under a microscope and named the tiny boxes he saw **cells**?
column14: Rudolf Virchow
column15: Robert Hooke
column16: Theodor Schwann
column17: Matthias Schleiden
column28: Robert Hooke looked at cork in 1665 and named the little boxes cells. Schleiden (plants, 1838), Schwann (animals, 1839), and Virchow (cells come from cells) all came much later and built on his discovery.
column29: Think of the earliest name on the cell theory timeline, the one who looked at cork.

column9: Which statement is one of the three parts of the cell theory?
column14: All cells have a nucleus.
column15: All cells are surrounded by a cell wall.
column16: All cells come from pre-existing cells.
column17: Cells can form from nonliving matter.
column28: All cells come from pre-existing cells is the third part of cell theory. Bacteria have no nucleus, animal cells have no cell wall, and cell theory says cells do NOT form from nonliving matter.
column29: Two of the wrong choices are true for some cells but not all cells. One goes against the theory completely.

column9: One part of the theory built by Schleiden, Schwann, and Virchow says that the ___ is the basic unit of structure and function in living things.
column28: The cell is the basic unit of structure and function of life. Organelles are smaller, but an organelle cannot live on its own; a cell can.
column29: It is bigger than an organelle and smaller than a tissue.

column9: Cell theory says that all living things are made of one or more cells.
column28: True. This is the first part of cell theory. A bacterium is made of one cell; you are made of trillions.
column29: Does the theory say "some" living things or "all" living things?

column9: Matthias Schleiden studied many different plant tissues. What did he conclude?
column14: All animals are made of cells.
column15: All cells come from pre-existing cells.
column16: Cork is made of tiny empty boxes.
column17: All plants are made of cells.
column28: Schleiden, a botanist, concluded that all plants are made of cells. Schwann said the same for animals a year later, Virchow said cells come from cells, and Hooke described the empty boxes in cork.
column29: Schleiden and Schwann split the living world in half. Schleiden took one half.

column9: In 1839, Theodor Schwann extended the cell idea to a second major group of living things. He concluded that all ___ are made of cells.
column28: Schwann studied animal tissues and concluded that all animals are made of cells. Put together with Schleiden's plant work, it supported the idea that all living things are made of cells.
column29: Schleiden's group and Schwann's group together covered almost all the living things scientists knew in 1839. Think of the two big groups people usually sort living things into.

column9: Which scientist is known for stating that **all cells come from pre-existing cells**?
column14: Robert Hooke
column15: Rudolf Virchow
column16: Anton van Leeuwenhoek
column17: Theodor Schwann
column28: Rudolf Virchow, a doctor who studied diseased tissue, stated that all cells come from pre-existing cells (1855). Hooke named cells, Leeuwenhoek saw living cells, and Schwann studied animal cells.
column29: He was a doctor, and he finished the cell theory with its third part.

column9: Which tool made the discovery of cells possible?
column14: The telescope
column15: The thermometer
column16: The microscope
column17: The balance
column28: Most cells are far too small to see with your eyes alone, so nobody knew cells existed until microscopes were good enough to show them.
column29: Cells are tiny. Which tool makes tiny things look bigger?

column9: Match each scientist to what he added to the cell theory.
column14: Robert Hooke :: Looked at cork and named the boxes cells
column15: Anton van Leeuwenhoek :: Made strong lenses and was first to see living single cells
column16: Matthias Schleiden :: Concluded that all plants are made of cells
column17: Theodor Schwann :: Concluded that all animals are made of cells
column18: Rudolf Virchow :: Stated that all cells come from pre-existing cells
column28: Hooke named cells (1665). Leeuwenhoek's lenses showed living single-celled organisms in pond water (1670s). Schleiden: plants (1838). Schwann: animals (1839). Virchow: cells come from cells (1855).
column29: Start with the pair you are surest of: Schleiden and Schwann split plants and animals.

column9: The cork cells Robert Hooke saw were living cells.
column28: False. Cork is dead plant tissue, so Hooke only saw the empty cell walls left behind, like an empty honeycomb. Leeuwenhoek was the first to see living cells.
column29: Where does cork come from, and can it still grow or respond?

column9: The old idea that living things can come from nonliving material is called spontaneous ___.
column28: Spontaneous generation was the old idea that life could pop out of nonliving things, like mice from grain. Virchow's part of cell theory, all cells come from pre-existing cells, replaced it.
column29: Spontaneous means "on its own." The missing word means producing or creating new life.

column9: Anton van Leeuwenhoek looked at a drop of pond water through lenses he ground himself. What is he known for?
column14: Being the first to see living single-celled organisms
column15: Naming the boxes in cork cells
column16: Showing that all plants are made of cells
column17: Stating that new cells come only from other existing cells
column28: Leeuwenhoek's lenses were strong enough to show tiny living things swimming in pond water, the first living cells anyone had seen. Naming cells was Hooke, plants were Schleiden, and cells from cells was Virchow.
column29: He looked at pond water, not cork. What would he see moving around?

column9: Kayla is sorting organisms for her cell theory notes into two groups: made of one cell, or made of many cells. Which of these organisms belongs in the one-cell group?
column14: An earthworm
column15: A mushroom
column16: A pine tree
column17: An amoeba
column28: An amoeba is a single cell. Earthworms, mushrooms, and pine trees are each made of many cells; a mushroom is a fungus whose body is built from many cells packed together. The cell theory covers both kinds: every living thing is made of one or more cells.
column29: Think about size. An organism made of just one cell is usually too small to see without a microscope.

column9: Which of these is NOT made of cells?
column14: A mushroom
column15: A bacterium
column16: A blade of grass
column17: A rock
column28: A rock is nonliving, so it is not made of cells. Mushrooms (fungi), bacteria, and grass are all living things, and the cell theory says every living thing is made of one or more cells.
column29: Cell theory is about living things. Which choice was never alive?

column9: Mr. Erickson's notes list the parts of the **modern** cell theory. Which statement is part of the modern cell theory but is NOT one of the original three parts?
column14: Cells contain genetic information (DNA, RNA).
column15: All living things are made of cells.
column16: All cells come from pre-existing cells.
column17: The cell is the basic unit of structure and function of life.
column28: The original three parts are: all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of structure and function, and all cells come from pre-existing cells. The modern cell theory adds that cells contain genetic information (DNA, RNA) and that all cells are similar in composition.
column29: Three of the choices are the original three parts. Which one talks about something scientists could not see until much later?

column9: Maya scrapes her knee. Two weeks later, new skin has covered the scrape. Which part of the cell theory does this healing best illustrate?
column14: All living things are made of cells.
column15: The cell is the basic unit of structure and function.
column16: All cells are similar in composition.
column17: All cells come from pre-existing cells.
column28: The new skin cells were made when the skin cells around the scrape divided. That is all cells come from pre-existing cells. The other parts are true, but they don't explain how the new skin got there.
column29: Ask what had to happen at the edges of the scrape to make the new skin.

column9: In the cell lab, Jaxon looks at onion skin, a scraping from inside his cheek, and a drop of pond water. He finds cells in the onion, in his cheek, and in every tiny organism swimming in the pond water. Which part of the cell theory do his observations support?
column14: All cells come from pre-existing cells.
column15: All living things are made of cells.
column16: Cells contain genetic information.
column17: All cells have a nucleus.
column28: He looked at a plant, an animal (himself), and pond organisms, and every one of them was made of cells. That supports all living things are made of cells. He did not watch cells divide or test for DNA, and the cell theory does not say every cell has a nucleus (bacteria don't).
column29: He looked at many DIFFERENT living things and found the same thing in each one.

column9: A virus is a piece of genetic material inside a protein coat. It has no cell membrane, no cytoplasm, and no ribosomes. According to the cell theory, how should a virus be classified?
column14: As living, because it has genetic material
column15: As not living, because it is not made of cells
column16: As living, because it can make people sick
column17: As a prokaryotic cell, because it has no nucleus
column28: A virus has no cell membrane, no cytoplasm, and no ribosomes, so it is not a cell. Cell theory says all living things are made of cells, so something that is not made of cells does not count as living. Having genetic material or causing disease isn't enough, and a virus isn't a prokaryote because it is not a cell at all.
column29: Compare what a virus has with what every cell has. Then check the virus against the first part of the cell theory.

column9: Which observations support the idea that **all cells come from pre-existing cells**? Select all that apply.
column14: A fertilized frog egg dividing into two cells, then four
column15: A yeast cell getting larger as it takes in sugar
column16: A bacterium splitting into two bacteria
column17: Onion root tip cells dividing under the microscope
column18: Finding cells in a mushroom, a moss, and a mouse
column19: A muscle cell contracting to help move an arm
column28: The frog egg, the bacterium, and the root tip cells each show an existing cell dividing to make new cells. A yeast cell getting bigger is growth, not a new cell. Finding cells in many organisms supports all living things are made of cells, and a muscle cell doing its job supports the cell as the basic unit of function. Neither shows where new cells come from.
column29: Look for an observation that shows where a NEW cell came from, not just that cells exist.

column9: Put the scientists in order, from earliest to latest, by when they added to the cell theory.
column14: Anton van Leeuwenhoek
column15: Robert Hooke
column16: Matthias Schleiden
column17: Theodor Schwann
column28: Hooke 1665, Leeuwenhoek 1670s, Schleiden 1838, Schwann 1839, Virchow 1855. Cells had to be discovered before anyone could say what is made of them, and that had to come before anyone could say where cells come from.
column29: Cells had to be seen before anyone could say plants and animals were made of them, and that came before anyone asked where cells come from.

column9: Schleiden and Schwann each studied a different group of living things. Which part of the cell theory did their work support when it was put together?
column14: All cells come from pre-existing cells.
column15: All living things are made of cells.
column16: Cells contain genetic information (DNA).
column17: Cells are the smallest units of matter.
column28: Plants plus animals covered most of the living world they knew, so together their work supported the first part: all living things are made of cells. Virchow added cells come from cells, and DNA came much later.
column29: Each one studied a different half of the living world, and both found the same thing. Put their conclusions together.

column9: Why was the third part of the cell theory, all cells come from pre-existing cells, such an important change in biology?
column14: It replaced the old idea that life can form from nonliving matter.
column15: It proved that every cell, including bacteria, has a nucleus.
column16: It showed that plants and animals are made of different materials.
column17: It explained how microscope lenses make tiny objects look larger.
column28: Before Virchow, many people believed in spontaneous generation, that life could come from nonliving matter. His idea said every cell has a parent cell. It had nothing to do with nuclei, plant vs. animal materials, or how microscopes work.
column29: Think about the old idea that this part of the theory replaced.

column9: According to the cell theory, a single-celled bacterium counts as a complete living thing.
column28: True. The cell is the basic unit of life, so one cell can be a whole organism. Bacteria, yeast, and paramecia are each made of just one cell and carry out every life process.
column29: Can one cell carry out all the processes of life by itself?

column9: During the pond water lab, Kenzie watched one paramecium (a single-celled organism) pinch in the middle and split into two paramecia. Which part of the cell theory does this best show?
column14: All living things are made of cells.
column15: All cells are similar in composition.
column16: Cells contain genetic information.
column17: All cells come from pre-existing cells.
column28: She watched one cell become two. Both new cells came from a cell that already existed, which is all cells come from pre-existing cells. The observation was about where new cells come from, not what living things or cells are made of.
column29: What did she actually watch happen: one becoming two.

column9: Nora reads that the cell is the **basic unit of structure and function** in living things. What does that mean?
column14: Living things are built from cells, and cells carry out all of life's jobs.
column15: Every cell in an organism looks exactly the same and does the same job.
column16: Cells are smaller than atoms, so they are the smallest unit of matter.
column17: Only multicellular organisms are made of cells; single cells are not alive.
column28: Structure means what something is built from; function means the jobs it does. Living things are built from cells, and their jobs (digesting, moving, growing) are done by cells. Cells are not all identical, they are much bigger than atoms, and single-celled organisms count too.
column29: Break it into two words: structure (what it is built of) and function (the jobs it does).

column9: Which discovery would **contradict** the cell theory?
column14: A new kind of bacterium found deep in the ocean
column15: A plant cell that is larger than most animal cells
column16: A living organism that is not made of any cells
column17: A single-celled organism that swims using a flagellum
column28: Cell theory says ALL living things are made of cells, so a living thing with no cells would go against it. A new bacterium, a large plant cell, and a swimming single cell are all still cells, so they fit the theory.
column29: For each choice, ask whether it is still a cell or still made of cells. A theory is only contradicted when one of its "all" statements fails.

column9: People have studied living things for thousands of years, but the cell theory did not appear until the 1800s. What is the best explanation?
column14: Scientists were not interested in studying living things before the 1800s.
column15: Cells did not exist until the 1600s, when they first appeared on Earth.
column16: Cells are too small to see, and microscopes took a long time to improve.
column17: Cells were too large to fit under the lenses of early microscopes.
column28: Most cells are far too small to see with the naked eye. Hooke's microscope first showed cells in 1665, and it took better lenses and many more observations before scientists could say that all plants and animals are made of cells.
column29: What tool did every cell scientist need, and when was it invented?

column9: According to the cell theory, which of these are made of cells? Select all that apply.
column14: A mushroom
column15: A virus
column16: An oak tree
column17: A bacterium
column28: Every living thing, from bacteria to oak trees, mushrooms, and humans, is made of one or more cells. A salt crystal is nonliving, and a virus is genetic material in a protein coat, not a cell.
column29: Living things are made of cells. Which two choices are not living things made of cells?

column9: Jamal compares a muscle cell, a skin cell, a leaf cell, and a bacterium. All four have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, and DNA. Which part of the modern cell theory does this support?
column14: All cells come from pre-existing cells.
column15: All cells are similar in composition.
column16: All cells have a nucleus.
column17: All living things are made of one cell.
column28: Very different cells are built from the same basic parts, which supports all cells are similar in composition. He did not watch cells divide, the bacterium has no nucleus, and many living things are made of many cells.
column29: He found the same parts in every cell. Which choice talks about what cells are made of?

column9: Abby looks at a thin slice of wood from an old wooden spoon under a microscope. She sees the walls of cells, even though the spoon is not alive. Does this go against the cell theory?
column14: Yes. It says only living things can have cells or cell walls.
column15: No. It says living things are made of cells, not that all cells are alive.
column16: Yes. The spoon's cells must have formed from nonliving wood.
column17: No. Anything made of cells is still alive, even a spoon.
column28: The cell theory says all living things are made of cells. It does not say that everything with cells is alive. The wood's cells were made by a living tree (from pre-existing cells) and died long ago. Nothing about the spoon breaks any part of the theory, and a spoon is not alive.
column29: Read the first part of the theory word for word. What does it promise, and what does it not promise?

column9: Cell theory says new cells can form from nonliving material as long as the conditions are right.
column28: False. Cell theory says all cells come from pre-existing cells. The idea that life forms from nonliving material is spontaneous generation, which the cell theory replaced.
column29: What does the third part of cell theory say every new cell needs?

column9: Which statements are part of the modern cell theory in Mr. Erickson's notes? Select all that apply.
column14: All cells contain a nucleus.
column15: All living things are made of cells.
column16: All cells contain chloroplasts.
column17: Cells contain genetic information (DNA, RNA).
column18: All cells come from pre-existing cells.
column19: All cells are similar in composition.
column28: The modern cell theory: the cell is the basic unit of structure and function, all living things are made of cells, all cells come from pre-existing cells, cells contain genetic information, and all cells are similar in composition. Bacteria have no nucleus, and animal cells have no chloroplasts.
column29: Test each statement against a bacterium and an animal cell. If either one breaks the rule, it is not part of the theory.

column9: Match each example to the part of the cell theory it shows best.
column14: A tree, a mushroom, and a bacterium are all built from cells :: All living things are made of cells
column15: A yeast cell divides to make a new yeast cell :: All cells come from pre-existing cells
column16: Your stomach digests food because its cells make enzymes :: The cell is the basic unit of structure and function
column17: A cell uses the instructions stored in its DNA to build proteins :: Cells contain genetic information
column28: Built from cells = all living things are made of cells. A cell making a new cell = cells come from pre-existing cells. Cells doing the body's jobs = basic unit of structure and function. Instructions stored in DNA = cells contain genetic information.
column29: Look for the key idea in each example: built from, divides, does a job, or DNA.

column9: A blue whale is made of about 100 quadrillion cells, and a bacterium is made of just one. How does the cell theory treat these two organisms?
column14: Only the whale counts, because one cell is too small to be alive.
column15: Both are living things made of cells, so the theory applies to both.
column16: Only the bacterium counts, because the theory is about single cells.
column17: Neither counts, because the theory applies only to plants.
column28: Cell theory says ALL living things are made of one or more cells. A one-celled bacterium and a 100-quadrillion-celled whale are both living, and the cell is the basic unit of life in each one.
column29: Does the theory say "one or more cells" or "many cells"?

column9: A scientist's claim about cells was accepted only after other scientists did the same observations again and got the same result. When other scientists redo an investigation and get the same result, it is called ___.
column28: Replication means other scientists redo an investigation and get the same result. One observation could be a fluke or a mistake; results that other scientists replicate can be trusted. That is how the cell theory became a theory.
column29: It comes from the same root as "replica," an exact copy.

column9: A scientist announces that she found a new organism in a hot spring that grows and reproduces but has no cells. What is the best response from other scientists?
column14: Throw out the cell theory right away, since one claim disproves it.
column15: Ignore the claim, because the cell theory can never be wrong.
column16: Decide the organism must be a virus without studying it further.
column17: Check her evidence first; if it holds up, revise the cell theory.
column28: Scientists don't throw out a theory backed by centuries of evidence after one claim, and they don't ignore new evidence either. They look again (replicate). If the claim holds up, the theory is revised to fit the new evidence.
column29: Good science neither ignores new evidence nor trusts one result right away.

column9: Sam says, "A virus has DNA, and cells have DNA, so the cell theory says a virus is alive." What is the best evaluation of Sam's argument?
column14: Correct: anything that contains DNA counts as a living cell.
column15: Correct: viruses come from other viruses, so they must be cells.
column16: Incorrect: DNA alone isn't enough; a virus is not made of cells.
column17: Incorrect: viruses have no genetic material of any kind.
column28: Cells contain DNA, but containing DNA does not make something a cell. A virus is only genetic material in a protein coat. It has no cell membrane or cytoplasm and can't carry out life processes on its own, so cell theory doesn't count it as living. Viruses DO have genetic material, so the last choice is wrong.
column29: "All cells have DNA" is not the same as "everything with DNA is a cell."

column9: Before the cell theory was complete, some scientists thought new cells formed out of the fluid between cells, the way crystals form in salt water. Which observation would best disprove this idea?
column14: Seeing that cells in a leaf are shaped like little boxes
column15: Finding that cork is made of empty cell walls left behind by dead cells
column16: Watching each new cell form when an existing cell divides in two
column17: Measuring that most cells are smaller than 0.1 mm across
column28: If every new cell is seen coming from a parent cell dividing, cells are not forming out of fluid. Box shapes, cork walls, and cell size don't tell you where new cells come from.
column29: The idea is about where new cells come from. Which observation shows where they come from?

column9: Liam says bacteria form on their own from chicken broth. He boils two flasks of broth to kill any bacteria. Which setup would best test his claim?
column14: Leave both flasks open to the air, then check each one for bacteria after a week.
column15: Add bacteria to both flasks and see which flask grows more bacteria.
column16: Boil the broth even longer, then check one flask for bacteria.
column17: Seal one flask, leave the other open to the air, and compare them after a week.
column28: If bacteria come only from pre-existing bacteria, the sealed flask should stay clear while the open flask (where bacteria from the air can land) gets cloudy. Leaving both open or adding bacteria to both can't separate the two ideas, and boiling longer with only one flask leaves nothing to compare it to.
column29: A fair test changes only one thing. If Liam is right, where do the bacteria come from? If the cell theory is right, where must they come from? Design flasks that tell those two apart.

column9: Why wasn't Hooke's discovery enough to support the statement that ALL living things are made of cells?
column14: He saw cells only in cork and a few other plants, never in animals.
column15: His microscope showed only living animal cells, not plant cells.
column16: He thought the boxes he saw were bubbles, not real cells.
column17: He studied only bacteria from pond water, not plants.
column28: Hooke described boxes in cork and in a few other plant stems, but he never described cells in animals or in most kinds of living things. A claim about ALL living things needed Schleiden's work on many plants and Schwann's work on many animals.
column29: In which kinds of living things did Hooke actually describe cells?

column9: A doctor finds a tumor that started in the tissue of a patient's lung. According to the cell theory, where did the tumor cells come from?
column14: From the patient's own lung cells dividing over and over
column15: From nonliving material in the air the patient breathed
column16: From the patient's DNA forming new cells by itself
column17: From the fluid between the lung cells hardening into cells
column28: All cells come from pre-existing cells, so tumor cells come from body cells that divide out of control. Virchow, a doctor, used diseased tissue like this as evidence. Cells don't form from air, loose DNA, or fluid.
column29: Use the third part of the cell theory. Which choices describe something that is not a cell turning into a cell?

column9: Tyler watches one bacterium under the microscope for 10 minutes and never sees it divide. This is good evidence against the idea that all cells come from pre-existing cells.
column28: False. Not seeing something happen in 10 minutes does not show that it never happens; many bacteria take 20 minutes or longer to divide, and some take hours. The observation also shows nothing forming from nonliving matter, so it gives no evidence against the idea that cells come from pre-existing cells.
column29: Ask what the observation actually shows, and what it does not show.

column9: Which set of observations would be the WEAKEST evidence for the statement "all living things are made of cells"?
column14: 40 samples from plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria, all made of cells
column15: Tissues from 25 different animals and 25 different plants, all made of cells
column16: Every organism found in water from 10 different ponds, all made of cells
column17: 300 slides of onion skin, all cut from the same onion, all made of cells
column28: 300 slides sounds like a lot, but every slide comes from one onion, one kind of organism. A claim about ALL living things needs evidence from many different kinds of living things, and each of the other sets covers many kinds: four big groups of life, 50 different plants and animals, or every organism in 10 ponds.
column29: Think about what the word ALL in the statement requires the evidence to cover.

column9: On Ty's cell theory timeline, the idea "all cells come from pre-existing cells" comes BEFORE cells were first named in cork. Why can't that be right?
column14: Cells had to be discovered before anyone asked where they come from.
column15: Ideas about animal cells always had to come before ideas about plant cells.
column16: Hooke's main idea was that cells come from nonliving matter.
column17: The microscope was invented by the scientist who said cells come from cells.
column28: You can't explain where cells come from until you know cells exist. Hooke named cells in 1665; Virchow stated cells come from pre-existing cells in 1855. Animal and plant cells were studied at almost the same time (1838 and 1839), Hooke never claimed cells come from nonliving matter, and Virchow didn't invent the microscope.
column29: Which idea depends on the other one already being known?

column9: Which statement best explains why the cell theory is called a scientific **theory**?
column14: It is a well-tested explanation backed by evidence from many scientists.
column15: It has been proven so many times that it can never be changed.
column16: It is a hypothesis that will become a law once it is fully proven.
column17: It is the opinion that most scientists agree with, even without evidence.
column28: A scientific theory is a well-tested explanation backed by a large body of evidence that many scientists have replicated. Even a strong theory stays open to new evidence, so "can never be changed" is wrong. Theories do not turn into laws: a law describes what happens, and a theory explains why. A theory is never just an opinion; evidence is the whole point.
column29: In science, the word theory means something different than it does in everyday talk. What does a scientific theory need behind it?

column9: Grace says, "Mold shows up on old bread out of nowhere, so cells can come from nonliving bread." Which response best uses the cell theory?
column14: Living mold spores landed on the bread and divided to make more mold.
column15: She is right: old bread slowly turns into living mold cells over time.
column16: Mold is not alive, so the cell theory does not apply to it.
column17: The bread's dead cells came back to life and became mold.
column28: Mold only seems to come from nowhere because its spores are too small to see. The spores are living cells that land on the bread and divide, so every mold cell came from a pre-existing cell. Mold is alive, and bread doesn't turn into mold.
column29: Where could invisible living cells have come from before the mold showed up?

column9: One of Ana's skin cells divides into two new skin cells. Which part of the modern cell theory best explains why both new cells know how to be skin cells?
column14: All living things are made of one or more cells.
column15: All cells come from pre-existing cells.
column16: Cells contain genetic information (DNA, RNA).
column17: All cells are similar in composition.
column28: The instructions for being a skin cell are stored in the DNA. Before dividing, the parent cell copies its DNA and gives a full copy to each new cell, so both know how to be skin cells. All cells come from pre-existing cells explains where the new cells came from, not how they got their instructions. Being made of cells and having similar parts don't explain the instructions either.
column29: The question is not where the new cells came from, but how they got their instructions.

column9: Which discoveries would force scientists to revise the cell theory? Select all that apply.
column14: A cell that has no nucleus
column15: A cell that formed from nonliving chemicals in a sealed jar
column16: A living organism that has no cells at all
column17: A new species of bacteria found in a cave
column18: A single cell large enough to see without a microscope
column19: An organism made of trillions of cells
column28: A living thing with no cells breaks "all living things are made of cells," and a cell forming from nonliving chemicals breaks "all cells come from pre-existing cells." New bacteria, cells with no nucleus (prokaryotes), huge organisms, and large single cells all still fit the theory.
column29: For each discovery, ask: does it break one of the parts of the theory, or is it just a new kind of cell?

column9: Lena puts 10 yeast cells in sugar water and counts them every 2 hours. Data table: Time (h): 0, 2, 4, 6 | Yeast cells: 10, 20, 40, 80. What does the pattern best show?
column14: The same number of cells forms out of the sugar every 2 hours.
column15: The yeast cells stop dividing after the first 2 hours.
column16: The count doubles every 2 hours, so each yeast cell divides into two.
column17: New yeast cells form from the water, not from other cells.
